slides.title: Chicago and San Diego weather comparison
slides.graph_reference: Original notebook cell 59, all temperature, precipitation, pressure, and wind panels together
slides.takeaway: Explore the two cities before choosing a modeling question
on_slide: Daily mean ERA5 data, 2009–2010
Nearest grid point to each city
slides.notes: I began by comparing Chicago and San Diego across temperature, precipitation, pressure, and wind. I used ERA5 daily means from 2009 and 2010 at the nearest grid points, exploring patterns before choosing a modeling question.

slides.title: Temperature patterns and sample maxima
slides.graph_reference: Original notebook cell 60, city temperature comparison and marked study-region maximum date
slides.takeaway: Chicago has much greater temperature variation in this sample
on_slide: Temperature SD: Chicago 10.90°C, San Diego 2.77°C
City maxima are daily means within these files
slides.notes: Chicago showed much greater temperature variation: a standard deviation of about 10.9 degrees Celsius, compared with 2.8 in San Diego. The highest city daily means were about 28.3 and 24.6 degrees. These are sample maxima, and two years do not establish a climate trend.

slides.title: Exploring a precipitation event
slides.graph_reference: Original notebook cell 61, stormiest-day precipitation and wind exploration
slides.takeaway: Rainfall conclusions remain limited by the precipitation scaling
on_slide: Study-region average uses a rectangular domain
Precipitation daily-total scaling remains unvalidated
slides.notes: I examined wind on the day with the largest displayed regional precipitation value. That average covers a rectangular study region. The precipitation scaling still needs validation as daily rainfall totals, which limits the rainfall conclusions.

slides.title: Predicting tomorrow’s temperature
slides.graph_reference: Original notebook cell 62, next-day forecasting comparison
slides.takeaway: A neural network did not consistently beat linear regression
on_slide: Current and lagged weather features predict tomorrow
Earlier 75% train, later 25% test
slides.notes: I first used current and lagged weather to predict tomorrow’s temperature, training on the earlier seventy-five percent of dates. Chicago’s linear and neural models both scored about 1.46 degrees. San Diego’s linear model scored 0.63, compared with 0.68 for the network. This used one chronological test split.

slides.title: Chicago seasonal prediction
slides.graph_reference: Original notebook cell 63, first image: Chicago training and 2010 evaluation side by side
slides.takeaway: Day of year predicts seasonal temperature, a different target from tomorrow’s weather
on_slide: Train on 2009, evaluate on 2010
Chicago linear/NN MAE: 8.91/2.92°C
slides.notes: I then asked whether day of year alone could capture the seasonal pattern. Training on 2009 and evaluating on 2010, Chicago’s error fell from 8.91 degrees with a straight line to 2.92 with the network.

slides.title: San Diego seasonal prediction
slides.graph_reference: Original notebook cell 63, second image: San Diego training and 2010 evaluation side by side
slides.takeaway: The network’s advantage is smaller in San Diego
on_slide: Same seasonal question and year split
San Diego linear/NN MAE: 1.68/1.48°C
slides.notes: I repeated the seasonal experiment for San Diego. Error fell from 1.68 degrees with the straight line to 1.48 with the network. The improvement was smaller here.

slides.title: Seasonal prediction in both cities
slides.graph_reference: Original notebook cell 64, combined Chicago and San Diego seasonal comparison
slides.takeaway: An alternative view of the same seasonal experiment
on_slide: Same results as the previous two city views
Different city patterns produce different model gains
slides.notes: This combined view shows the same seasonal experiment as the previous two slides. It makes the larger improvement in Chicago easier to compare.

slides.title: Monthly validation: 5, 10 and 20 neurons
slides.takeaway: Monthly holdouts evaluate gaps throughout the 2009 seasonal curve
on_slide: Final seven days of every month held out
281 training days, 84 validation days
slides.notes: To compare network settings across all seasons, I held out the final seven days of every month in 2009. That left 281 training days and 84 validation days. These curves compare five, ten, and twenty neurons on identical dates. This changes the evaluation question, so lower errors cannot be compared directly with the 2010 results.

slides.title: Training and validation errors
slides.takeaway: Lowest validation MAE occurs at different widths for the two cities
on_slide: Chicago: 10 neurons, MAE 2.498°C
San Diego: 20 neurons, MAE 1.183°C
slides.notes: The bars compare training and validation error. More neurons improved training fit, but did not consistently improve validation. Chicago’s lowest validation error was about 2.50 degrees with ten neurons, almost tied with twenty. San Diego’s was about 1.18 with twenty. I chose settings using validation error.

slides.title: Comparing single networks and ensembles
slides.graph_reference: week6_ensemble_results/ensemble_comparison.png, original six-panel figure with member spread
slides.takeaway: The ensemble did not lower either city’s best single-model MAE
on_slide: Five fixed random seeds per network size
Member spread measures disagreement between fits
slides.notes: I averaged five networks with different initial weights to test whether predictions became more reliable. The ensemble did not lower either city’s best single-model MAE. The shaded spread shows disagreement between fits, not calibrated weather uncertainty.

slides.title: Effect of L2 penalty strength
slides.takeaway: Stronger regularization does not steadily reduce validation error
on_slide: Alpha controls the penalty on large weights
One fitted solution does not establish a universal ranking
slides.notes: I also tested six L2 penalty strengths. Alpha penalizes large weights, but stronger penalties did not steadily lower validation error. San Diego’s twenty-neuron model spiked at one setting. Different penalties can lead training to different fits, and initialization can change the ranking.

slides.title: Seasonal fits before and after L2 tuning
slides.takeaway: Four models retain their original penalty and overlapping curves
on_slide: Original models already use alpha 0.0001
Compare each width with its validation-selected penalty
slides.notes: These panels compare original fits with their validation-selected penalties. The originals already used weak L2 regularization. Four models kept their original setting, so their curves overlap. Stronger penalties did not consistently improve every model.

slides.title: Before and after L2: error comparison
slides.graph_reference: week6_regularization_results/before_after_l2.png, original four-panel training and validation figure
slides.takeaway: San Diego’s 10-neuron model improves, while overall MAE winners stay unchanged
on_slide: San Diego 10: validation MAE 1.283 to 1.209°C
Training MAE 1.151 to 1.189°C
Independent evaluation is needed to confirm the gain
slides.notes: The clearest L2 change was San Diego’s ten-neuron network. Validation error fell from about 1.28 to 1.21 degrees, while training error rose slightly. A closer training fit was therefore unnecessary for better predictions on these held-out weeks.

slides.title: Conclusions: what we tested and learned
slides.graph_reference: Concluding synthesis of the preceding city comparisons and model experiments
slides.takeaway: The benefit of model complexity depends on the city and prediction task
on_slide: The neural network does not consistently improve the next-day forecast
Seasonal curvature is learned better than a straight line
Monthly validation selects 10 neurons for Chicago and 20 for San Diego
L2 improves San Diego 10-neuron validation MAE by 5.8%, but overall MAE winners stay unchanged
The ensemble does not lower the best single-model MAE
slides.notes: The results depend on the task and city. Chicago showed stronger seasonal variability. The neural network learned seasonal curvature better than a straight line, but did not consistently improve the next-day forecast. Monthly validation selected ten neurons for Chicago and twenty for San Diego. L2 reduced San Diego’s ten-neuron validation MAE by about 5.8 percent, but the lowest-MAE overall choices stayed unchanged. Ensembles also failed to beat the best single-model MAE.

slides.title: Limitations and future exploration
slides.graph_reference: Limitations and next steps for the preceding analyses
slides.takeaway: Independent evaluation, stronger baselines, and data checks are needed to confirm conclusions
on_slide: L2 tuning uses 2009 and one initialization: repeat seeds and evaluate untouched years
Validation reuse and correlated days: separate final test and chronological forecasting evaluation
Calendar-only inputs and weak linear baseline: sine/cosine seasonal features and richer weather predictors
Two-year climate sample and unvalidated rainfall totals: longer records and unit checks
slides.notes: The monthly results reconstruct 2009 gaps. One training year and one L2 initialization limit robustness. Reusing validation for selection and reporting, alongside related neighboring days, requires a separate final test. I would repeat seeds, use untouched years, and evaluate forecasts chronologically. Calendar-only inputs and the weak straight-line baseline motivate sine and cosine features and richer weather predictors. Two years cannot establish climate trends, and rainfall totals need unit checks. Longer records would strengthen these conclusions.
